extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and advanced law students researching computation of profits in patent-infringement suits
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for determining and proving the profits recoverable by a patentee from a defendant who has used or manufactured and used the patented invention, including what receipts/savings are chargeable, allowable deductions, apportionment, burden of proof, and temporal scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual receipts and savings alone regarded
rubrics_metrics.description: Only elements actually saved or actually received by the defendant, in money or some form of property having definite ascertainable monetary value, may enter into the computation of profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude intangible or non-pecuniary benefits (e.g., increased comfort, intellectual acquisitions). Profits must be susceptible of computation or estimation. (See §1146 and cases cited such as Vaaghan v. Central Pacific R.R. Co., Piper v. Brown.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude remote and contingent profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Remote or contingent gains depending on future bargains, speculations, or other uncertain events are not recoverable as profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery is limited to profits resulting directly or immediately from the wrongful act; future speculative profits are rejected. (See §1146, §1147 and Piper v. Brown.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant treated as trustee for realized profits
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringer who has wrongfully used the patentee's invention is treated as a trustee and must account for receipts and savings actually made by reason of the use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not a valid defense for the infringer to show he might have made equal profits by using his own invention or a third party's invention; the trustee doctrine requires accounting for what was actually gained. (Authorities cited in §1146.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable deductions from receipts (expenses of use)
rubrics_metrics.description: When receipts are compensation for unlawful use, profits are the gross receipts less expenses attendant on the use—power, labor, salaries, shop-rent, value of use of buildings, tools, other property necessary to the infringing act, current running expenses, waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deduct the value of the infringer's personal time and skill or losses in other branches of business. Details and examples appear in §1147 and §1148 (list of allowed items: machinery, power, materials, wages, storage, freight, commissions, repairs, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When receipts are prices for products, apportion by attributable market value
rubrics_metrics.description: If the product's market value is entirely derived from elements resulting from the infringing process or device, total receipts may be attributed to the infringement; otherwise divide the price in the ratio of the market values due to infringing and extraneous elements, and treat only the portion attributable to the infringing elements as receipts from the unlawful use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduct the proportionate cost of making and marketing the product (rental, machinery, materials, wages, freight, commissions, tools, repairs, waste, share of current expenses). If the infringing elements only account for a fraction of value, only that fraction is chargeable. (See §1148.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental sales/profits attributable to invention must be credited
rubrics_metrics.description: If use of the infringing elements increased sales to a definitely measurable extent, all profit from that increment of sales must be attributed to the use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if no direct per-unit profit appears after ordinary deductions, a measurable increase in sales attributable to the invention yields profits equal to the additional profit from those sales. (See §1148.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare net receipts to what defendant would have earned using prior public processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute what the defendant would have received net (price less costs) had he used an instrument or process that was open to the public prior to conception of the patented invention; the difference between actual net receipts and that hypothetical net indicates the profit from the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior open process would have produced a substantially identical marketable product, attribute only the difference as profit. If no open alternative existed, the net amount from the unlawful use is chargeable. (See §1148.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate profits attributable to improvements vs original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant's device embodies both the patented improvement and prior or other elements, profits due to the improvement must be separated from those due to the original or other contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plaintiff's patent covers only a feature, the proof must separate profit due to that feature; otherwise only nominal damages may be awarded. Allowances must be made for other contributory improvements. (See §1148 and cited cases such as Hurlbut v. Schillinger.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Savings of cost count as profits only if they increase gain or diminish loss
rubrics_metrics.description: A saving in the expense of manufacturing or marketing a product is included in profits if it produces a real gain or reduces loss; where product price equals cost, the saving is an escape from loss and thus a profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In general businesses where savings are distributed across many items, credit what can be shown by direct evidence or fair inference from the enterprise's nature. In loss-making enterprises, any saved loss that would have occurred without the invention is to be reckoned as profit. (See §1149 and Elizabeth v. Pavement Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's burden of proof — establish receipts/savings by reliable tangible proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must prove the existence and amount of receipts or savings by reliable and tangible evidence; each stage of computation must use arithmetical processes based on testimony and data furnished by the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff cannot disclose by evidence, he cannot claim those profits, though legal presumptions favor plaintiffs in willful infringement and reasonable calculations based on available data are acceptable, especially where defendant conceals facts. (See §1150 and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportion defendant's profits to the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must apportion the defendant's total profits and show what portion resulted from the patented invention; failure to do so may limit recovery to nominal damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the patent covers only one feature of a device, proof must separate the profit due to that feature; courts will not award unconscionable personal-service deductions to defendants trying to reduce shown profits. (See §1150 and authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits from subordinate methods: commissions, repairs, agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits derived through subordinate channels (commission agents, repair work, selling on commission) are recoverable to the extent they were distinct profits of the infringing use — commissions less apportioned general expenses; wages for repair less repair costs (excluding personal service value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If purchaser paid essentially the same price as plaintiff would have charged, the advantage contains no element of profit due to infringement (remedy is damages). Commission agents and sellers acting on behalf of principals may be sued; confusion-of-goods doctrine does not apply where there is only confusion of accounts. (See §1151.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of profits and interest — account to date of accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff is entitled to recover all profits derived by the defendant through infringing acts from the issue or re-issue date of the patent until the date of the accounting, irrespective of royalties the plaintiff paid to a licensor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether interest is recoverable and for what period depends on how profits accrued (legal vs equitable remedies). Accounts are taken to the time fixed by the bill; antedated patents make defendants liable from the antedated time; value of an infringement is measured at date of infringement. Assignees may recover entire profits despite prior royalty arrangements. (See §1152 and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No profits where defendant actually made none; remedy may be damages
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant through unskilfulness or business losses actually realized no profits from the infringing use, profits are not recoverable; the patentee's remedy in such case is ordinary damages rather than an accounting for profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not award profits where none are shown to exist; reasonable certainty is required but may be relaxed where defendant's concealment makes proof difficult. (See §1146, §1149, §1150 and cited cases like Conover v. Mers.)
